# Supported functions

<!-- Generated by `bun scripts/xlsx/function-list.ts` in src/core; do not edit by hand. -->

The calculation engine implements 501 functions. 379 of them appear in tests whose
expected values were recorded from real Excel (`src/core/xlsx/formula/__fixtures__`); the rest are
covered by unit tests only, with expected values worked out by hand or from documentation.
A function missing from this list returns `#NAME?`.

Verification: **Excel** means at least one recorded Excel result uses the function (it may be
nested in a larger formula, and one case does not prove every argument combination);
**Unit** means unit tests only.

| `FORECAST.ETS` | `FORECAST.ETS(target_date, values, timeline, [seasonality], [data_completion], [aggregation])` | Excel | The filter, starting values and error statistics were identified against Excel on 34 series: 10 reproduce to the last digit, typical series are within 0.5%, the worst is 9% (zero-filled gaps; the seasonal calls on SUM-aggregated duplicates are within 5%; with a season of 0 every aggregation is exact). Excel's search for alpha, beta and gamma minimises the squared one-step error of the training part plus the squared forecast error of the hold-out (the last 40% of the series, at most the larger of 10, two seasons and 20%; scale, offset and sign do not matter) and lands on a coarse lattice of values: without a season this reproduces its alpha on 471 of 491 non-seasonal probes (148 of 153 with 8 to 16 points), 134 of 136 spikes and steps and 421 of 484 series morphing from a random walk to noise, and 87% of the forecasts exactly (the worst is 11%). It does not reproduce Excel's choice of a beta above the lowest value (90% agree), an alpha of 1/6 on a family of bimodal 40-point series, or the 3 of 431 matching series where Excel's error statistics for an alpha of 0.998 follow some other rule (its forecasts there are the last value plus the least-squares slope, which is reproduced); with a season of 4 whole seasons or of 5 and more the same cost is used, since the starting states are then Excel's own, and elsewhere the plain one-step error. Starting states: the starting trend is exact (recovered to 1e-15 from Excel's forecasts) for every series without a season, 3 to 16 points. For seasonal series the start is a fixed linear function of the data, recovered exactly (ets-init-chain.ts, ets-init-chain.test.ts): for 4 whole seasons or 5 and more (only the first 5 seasons are read) the position states follow each other along m consecutive times through first-seasons means and half-split slopes of the positions and the start trend is the least-squares slope of the series without them, which reproduces Excel's forecasts at its own parameters to rounding error on about 1200 probe series (seasons 2 to 12). Not exact: 4 seasons plus a partial one (a mean over the windows of 4 whole seasons, within 2.5% of Excel's forecasts at its parameters), and 3 seasons or fewer, whose rule is still unknown (least squares, up to 28% off). Ruled out against the recovered maps: single and multi-pass backcasting with fixed parameters on a 0.01 lattice, weighted regressions with geometric weights, plain seasonal-dummy regression and classical decomposition. |
| `FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT` | `FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT(target_date, values, timeline, [confidence_level], [seasonality], [data_completion], [aggregation])` | Excel | RMSE times sqrt(1 + sum of (alpha + j*beta)^2) as in Excel: equal to Excel where the fitted parameters are, up to 37% off where they differ (mostly seasonal models, whose gamma term was not checked against Excel). |
| `FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY` | `FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY(values, timeline, [data_completion], [aggregation])` | Excel | First peak of the autocorrelation of the detrended series that reaches 0.3 (lags 2 to a third of the series); agrees with Excel on 113 of 126 recorded series, all noiseless waves, trends and impulse trains included. 0 means none. Excel also reports a period on about a third of short white-noise series (8 to 36 points) by a rule that is not the autocorrelation, and this does not. The noise picks of Excel do not follow the best-fitting seasonal ETS either (checked for periods up to 8), nor the lowest hold-out cost of the seasonal fit made here, nor the largest autocorrelation, periodogram peak or differenced autocorrelation (the period is the lag of the largest autocorrelation on 6 of the 10 noisy series where Excel reports one, but the same statistic is as large on series where it reports none). |
| `FORECAST.ETS.STAT` | `FORECAST.ETS.STAT(values, timeline, statistic_type, [seasonality], [data_completion], [aggregation])` | Excel | Step size agrees; the error statistics are measured on the last points as in Excel and equal it where the parameters do (11 of 32 series); alpha is found on 16 of 34 series, beta on 29 and gamma on 27 (on the 491 non-seasonal probes: alpha on 471, beta on 443). |
